I ran out of search and fetch requests before I could get past the most basic sources. I fully read only two pages: Guzik's Enduring Word commentary (the text broke off at verse 24) and the first part of the Precept Austin page (verse 1 and Ryle on verses 1–13). The rest comes from search-result excerpts of Precept Austin, Enduring Word and Matthew Henry. **I found nothing for parts 2 and 3.** I couldn't reach Lutheran, Methodist, Pentecostal or Catholic/Orthodox writers, NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, or any prosperity or hyper-grace teaching. Verses with no note had nothing on the pages I read.

## Part 1: The traditional reading

**v. 1:** Guzik sees this as a second official group from Jerusalem, after Mark 3:22. He thinks checking out Jesus was fine in itself, but they did it wrongly: their minds were already made up, and they didn't measure Him against God's Word. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-7/
- Hiebert (quoted on Precept Austin) thinks it probably happened in or near Capernaum. Constable says the clash helped prompt Jesus to leave Galilee again (v. 24). https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-7-commentary

**vv. 2–4:** Guzik says the leaders meant elaborate ceremonial washing, not washing to get clean, and observant Jews followed a strict and detailed ritual before meals. Quoting Lane, he says the priests' washing in Exodus 30:19 and 40:12 is where the wider custom came from. A very strict Jew washed between courses too, and the rabbis said bread eaten with unwashed hands was no better than excrement. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-7/
- Matthew Henry says the washing came before formal meals over which a blessing was said. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_007.cfm
- Ryle (Anglican) sees here how low Jewish religion had sunk: the holiest man was the one most careful about outward rules that people had made up. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-7-commentary

**v. 5:** Guzik notes that tradition, not Scripture, required these washings, and the leaders knew it but criticised the disciples anyway. He separates the written law from the oral law. Some leaders valued the oral law more highly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-7/
- Brian Bell (on Precept Austin) counts "tradition" six times in verses 3–13. He says tradition must serve Scripture, not the other way round. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-7-commentary

**vv. 6–7:** Guzik explains that "hypocrite" first meant an actor wearing a mask. He calls passing off human rules as God's teaching "one of the pillars of legalism." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-7/
- Henry: they stopped at the outside of religion, so their worship was in vain. God wasn't pleased with it and they gained nothing from it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_007.cfm
- Precept Austin connects "lips" and "heart" here to the teaching on the heart in verses 14–23. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-7-commentary
- Bell calls verse 7 the key verse of the section. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-7-commentary

**vv. 8–9:** Guzik's "second pillar" of legalism: first add human rules to God's Word, then reject God's command. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-7/
- Henry says they first treated God's commands as minor next to their traditions, then cancelled them when the two clashed. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_007.cfm

**v. 10:** Guzik: children must obey parents while young, and honour them all their lives. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-7/
- Henry: if cursing parents deserved death, letting them starve is far worse. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_007.cfm

**vv. 11–12:** Guzik: by calling his goods "Corban" (devoted to God), a son could keep them from his parents and look very religious while disobeying the command. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-7/

**v. 13:** Precept Austin: the Greek verb shows an ongoing habit, and Corban is just one example of many traditions that set the written Law aside. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-7-commentary

**v. 14:** Henry: Jesus said this part publicly because it touched everyday life. It isn't enough for people to hear; they must understand. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_007.cfm
- Precept Austin says verses 14–23 are teaching in parable form. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-7-commentary

**vv. 15–16:** Guzik: this doesn't mean nothing we take in can defile us; he gives pornography as an example. Here Jesus means ritual cleanness of food, looking ahead to Acts 10:15. Barclay (quoted by Guzik) called this nearly the most revolutionary passage in the New Testament. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-7/
- Ryle: moral purity doesn't depend on washing, touching or eating. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-7-commentary

**vv. 18–19:** Precept Austin's summary: defilement is a matter of the heart, not the stomach. Wuest's translation of verse 19 ends "making all the foods clean." https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-7-commentary
- Expositor's Greek Testament (quoted on Precept Austin) goes further. It says Jesus here criticises Moses as well as the scribes and "introduces a religious revolution." https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-7-commentary

**vv. 20–23:** Guzik calls this a 13-part list of the evil in the human heart. He quotes Spurgeon that "Sin is not a splash of mud upon man's exterior." Barclay (quoted by Guzik) says every sinful act starts with an inner choice. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-7/
- Ryle: Jesus means every human heart, not just notorious sinners. "The seeds of all the evils here mentioned lie hid within us all." https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-7-commentary
- Barclay on the Greek word for "greed": a lust for having things in someone who looks for happiness in things instead of God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews

**v. 24:** Constable (on Precept Austin): this is Jesus' first time outside Palestine. He did more Gentile ministry as more Jews rejected Him. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-7-commentary
- Henry: Christ was too well known to stay hidden for long. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_007.cfm
- Guzik quotes Barclay: after wiping out the line between clean and unclean foods, Jesus may here be wiping out the line between clean and unclean people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-7/

**vv. 25–26:** Precept Austin: Mark stresses her sex, race and origin, "three strikes" in Jewish eyes. "Kept asking" pictures her pleading again and again, and shows some faith in His power over demons. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-7-commentary
- Ryle: we know nothing about her beyond these verses. She is an example of persevering in prayer for others. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-7-commentary

**v. 27:** Guzik: "children" means the Jews and "dogs" means Gentiles. Jesus seemed to discourage her, but He used a softer word, "little dogs." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-7/

**v. 28:** Guzik: she accepts her low place yet trusts Him for crumbs. This shows that humble faith, coming as we are, wins. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-7/
- A commentator quoted on Precept Austin: Mark doesn't use the word "faith," but her answer shows exactly the faith Jesus valued. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-7-commentary

**vv. 29–30:** Precept Austin: "this answer" is literally "this word." Matthew adds praise for her great faith. The perfect tense means the demon left and stayed gone. This is the only healing in Mark done at a distance without a spoken command. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-7-commentary
- MacArthur (quoted there) thinks God was drawing her to salvation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-7-commentary

**vv. 31–35:** Guzik: the healing echoes Isaiah 35:5–6, showing the Messiah has come. Mark uses a rare Greek word to make the link clear. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-7/
- Henry: Jesus took him aside to avoid show and seeking glory. He used His own fingers and saliva because He alone heals. He looked up to heaven to give His Father the praise. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_007.cfm

**v. 36:** Henry: the order to keep quiet was humility and an example of self-denial for us. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_007.cfm

**v. 37:** Precept Austin's resources page lists sermons on this verse by Criswell ("He Hath Done All Things Well") and Hastings ("Admiration or Adoration"). I didn't read them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-7-resources

## Part 2: Where Protestant traditions differ

I found no real disagreement between Protestant traditions on this chapter. Two loosely related points:
- **Tradition (vv. 3–13):** Henry (Puritan, Presbyterian) uses the passage to attack "Papists." He says their zeal for church councils and canons is really zeal for power, as with the Pharisees. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_007.cfm Ryle (Anglican) warns about churches reduced to "unmeaning forms" and man-made fasts and feasts. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-7-commentary I couldn't get the Catholic or Orthodox side, so this is only one side of the argument.
- **Christian liberty (v. 7):** Guzik says practices Scripture doesn't command are matters of conscience; just don't look down on others either way. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-7/

## Part 3: Other views

- **"Faith for others" (v. 29):** A sermon quoted on Precept Austin, author not clear from the excerpt, says it was the mother's faith that brought the healing. If you can't muster "mega-faith," trust in the faith of those around you, because God honours it on your behalf. This lines up with debated "faith" teaching, but the page doesn't call it that. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-7-commentary
- I found nothing for modern scholarship, Catholic or Orthodox readings, or prosperity and word-of-faith teaching.

If you want me to keep going, next I'd look at the NET Bible note on verse 19, catholic.com or newadvent.org on tradition (vv. 8–13) and the Ephphatha rite in baptism (v. 34), and Lutheran sources on Ephphatha.
